newsitem.title: KENYA: Cheserem re-appointed Kenya central bank governor.
newsitem.headline: Cheserem re-appointed Kenya central bank governor.

text.p: Central Bank of Kenya (CBK) Governor Micah Cheserem, a leading figure in Kenya's economic reform process, was re-appointed to another four-year term on Thursday in a move that will calm markets in a turbulent election year.
"President (Daniel arap) Moi has re-appointed Mr Cheserem to another four-year term," said Mark Lesiit, personal assistant to the governor.
The reappointment should help to calm local financial markets which are nervous in the run up to a general election due before the end of 1997.

Foreign exchange and equity markets were severely jolted this month when police violently dispersed demonstrators at a rally called to press for constitutional reforms before presidential and parliamentary elections.
Lesiit told Reuters by telephone that Cheserem's re-appointment took effect on Thursday and would be formally announced in the official government gazette on Friday.
Cheserem, aged 47, took over as governor in July 1993 at the height of financial mismanagement in Kenya's banking system and accusations of corruption at the central bank.
He moved to restore discipline, helping to reduce money supply and cut inflation to current single-digit figures from around 101 percent in October 1993.
Investors had feared Cheserem's term would not be renewed because of his tough approach, which they said would prevent the government from manipulating finances during the 1997 polls.

In the aftermath of the July 7 violence, in which at least nine people were killed, Cheserem emerged as one of the key leaders that urged the government to seek dialogue as a means of ending the political stalemate.
"The actions of July 7 will not be repeated. We are moving fast. We want a stable country fit for all to invest and live in peacefully," Cheserem told a media reception on Wednesday.
"In future, it is likely that police will walk behind demonstrators to protect them rather than harass them. That is the way to go," Cheserem added.

Opposition leaders accused the government of printing cash before the December 1992 elections to help finance Moi's win. The result was spiralling inflation and interest rates of up to 85 percent and the shilling falling to as low as 84 versus the dollar.

A career accountant, the governor was commercial director of Lever Brothers Malawi Ltd and other Unilever Group subsidiaries in Malawi when he was called to replace Eric Kotut, under whose reign financial abuse became rampant and bad management thrived.
